explanation: Koalas evolved fingerprints separately from primates, probably to help grip branches and handle eucalyptus leaves. The ridges form loops and whorls much like ours.

claims.text: Koalas have fingerprints that closely resemble human fingerprints.
Kangaroos, wombats and Tasmanian devils do not have human-like fingerprints.
Koala fingerprints evolved independently of primate fingerprints.
Koala fingerprints may help them grip branches and handle food.
Koala fingerprint ridges form loops and whorls like human ones.

evidence.restatement: Koalas have finger ridges that are very hard to tell from human fingerprints (Henneberg and colleagues, 1996).
Among the four marsupials offered, only the koala is known for human-like fingerprints.
Koala fingerprints evolved convergently; their close relatives and most marsupials lack them.
The ridges are thought to aid grip when climbing and handling leaves.
Koala print ridges show loops, whorls and arches like human prints.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: A Wikipedia article on fingerprints reports that according to one study, even with an electron microscope, it can be quite difficult to distinguish between the fingerprints of a koala and a human. A PNAS paper on grip notes that fingerprints are unique to primates and koalas.

claimResults.note: Wikipedia (Fingerprint) and a PNAS paper on grip both single out koalas as the only non-primates with fingerprints; the first says even electron microscopy struggles to separate koala from human prints.

evidence.restatement: Among Australian marsupials only the koala is known for human-like fingerprints; kangaroos, wombats and Tasmanian devils are not.

claimResults.note: The search did not mention wombats or kangaroos directly, but the PNAS line that fingerprints are unique to primates and koalas agrees.

evidence.restatement: Koalas and primates are only distantly related, so koala fingerprints arose independently (convergent evolution).
Fingerprint ridges are thought to improve grip; for koalas that fits climbing and handling leaves, and the claim is hedged with "may".
Koala fingerprint patterns include the loops and whorls seen in human prints.
